'''''Trifolium pratense''''' (from Latin prātum, meaning meadow), '''red clover''',<ref name=BSBI07>{{BSBI 2007 |access-date=2014-10-17 }}</ref><ref>{{PLANTS|id=TRPR2|taxon=Trifolium pratense|access-date=15 December 2015}}</ref> is a [[herbaceous plant|herbaceous]] species of [[flowering plant]] in the bean family, [[Fabaceae]]. It is native to the [[Old World]], but planted and naturalised in many other regions.
==Description==
The red clover is a [[herbaceous]], short-lived [[perennial]] plant, which is generally variable in size, growing to {{convert|20–80|cm|0|abbr=on}} tall. It has a deep [[taproot]] which makes it tolerant to drought and gives it a good soil structuring effect.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://extension.psu.edu/red-clover|title=Red Clover|website=extension.psu.edu|language=en|access-date=2018-03-14}}</ref> The [[leaves]] are alternate, trifoliate (with three leaflets), each leaflet {{convert|15–30|mm|in|1|abbr=on|frac=8}} long and {{convert|8–15|mm|abbr=on|frac=8}} broad, green with a characteristic pale crescent in the outer half of the leaf. The [[Petiole (botany)|petiole]] is {{convert|1-4|cm|1|abbr=on|frac=4}} long, with two basal [[stipule]]s that are abruptly narrowed to a bristle-like point.
The [[flower]]s are dark pink with a paler base, {{convert|12–15|mm|in|1|abbr=on|frac=8}} long, produced in a dense [[inflorescence]]. In individual flowers, sepals are fused from the base into a hairy calyx tube with 5 teeth. The typical family 5 petals (standard, 2 wings and 2 keel) are also joined together at the base, and are up to 3 times longer than the calyx. The upper of the 10 stamens is free, with the filaments of the 9 other joined into a tube surrounding the style.<ref name="CTW1968">{{cite book |last1=Clapham |first1=A. R. |last2=Tutin |first2=T. G. |last3=Warburg |first3=E. F. |title=Excursion Flora of the British Isles |date=1968 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |pages=148–160 |edition=2nd}}</ref> They are mostly visited by [[bumblebee]]s.<ref>{{Cite journal | doi = 10.1111/plb.12328| pmid = 25754608| title = Competition for pollinators and intra-communal spectral dissimilarity of flowers| journal = Plant Biology| volume = 18| issue = 1| pages = 56–62| year = 2015| last1 = Van Der Kooi | first1 = C. J.| last2 = Pen | first2 = I.| last3 = Staal | first3 = M.| last4 = Stavenga | first4 = D. G.| last5 = Elzenga | first5 = J. T. M.|url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/273158762| hdl = 11370/caee8d0d-9724-4056-9d45-93162a5a7afc| hdl-access = free}}</ref>
Cultivated varieties are substantially larger than the wild plants.<ref name="WFK2006">{{cite book |last1=Rose |first1=Francis |last2=O'Reilly |first2=Clare |title=The Wild Flower Key |date=2006 |publisher=Penguin Books Ltd |page=274}}</ref>

== Taxonomy ==
{{missing information|section|infraspecific classification: particularly the ''sativum'' variety mentioned below<!--  Kew lists three subspecies but also notes that classification is "complex". -->|date=February 2022}}
''Trifolium pratense'' was initially published by [[Carl Linnaeus]] in his book ''[[Species Plantarum]]'' (1753).<ref>p. 768.</ref>
The genus has 3 known subspecies:<ref name="Worldflora">{{cite web |title=Trifolium pratense L. |url=https://www.worldfloraonline.org/taxon/wfo-0000213053 |access-date=4 August 2023}}</ref>
*''Trifolium pratense'' subsp. ''baeticum'' {{Au|(Boiss.) Vicioso}}
*''Trifolium pratense'' subsp. ''kotulae'' {{au|(Pawl.) Soják}}
*''Trifolium pratense'' subsp. ''pratense''
==Distribution==
The red clover is native to Europe, Western Asia, and northwest Africa, but it has been [[naturalisation (biology)|naturalised]] in other continents, like North and South America. Specifically, the red clover was brought to [[Argentina]] and [[Chile]] over 100 years ago, although it is not clear how exactly it was introduced.<ref>{{Cite journal|title = Evaluation of Introduced and Naturalised Populations of Red Clover(Trifolium pratense L.) at Pergamino EEA-INTA, Argentina|journal = Genetic Resources and Crop Evolution|date = 2005-08-01|issn = 0925-9864|pages = 507–511|volume = 52|issue = 5|doi = 10.1007/s10722-005-0777-z|first1 = B. S.|last1 = Rosso|first2 = E. M.|last2 = Pagano| bibcode=2005GRCEv..52..507R |s2cid = 21172324}}</ref> Additionally, it has been introduced to New Zealand.<ref name="Morales-2013">{{Cite journal|title = Rapid ecological replacement of a native bumble bee by invasive species|journal = Frontiers in Ecology and the Environment|date = 2013-07-15|issn = 1540-9295|pages = 529–534|volume = 11|issue = 10|doi = 10.1890/120321|first1 = Carolina L|last1 = Morales|first2 = Marina P|last2 = Arbetman|first3 = Sydney A|last3 = Cameron|first4 = Marcelo A|last4 = Aizen| bibcode=2013FrEE...11..529M |s2cid = 86469248}}</ref>
== Ecology ==
[[File:Bombus schrencki - Trifolium pratense - Keila.jpg|thumb|Red clover is a good pollen and nectar source for bumblebees]]
One important pollinator, which was also brought from Europe, is ''[[Large garden bumblebee|Bombus ruderatus]]'', or the large garden bumblebee. This bumblebee has been one of the important pollinators of red clover in South America and New Zealand.<ref name="Morales-2013" />
Red clover is subject to bacterial as well as fungal [[List of red clover diseases|diseases]], including clover rot,<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Öhberg |first1=H. |last2=Bång |first2=U. |date=2010 |title=Biological control of clover rot on red clover by ''Coniothyrium minitans'' under natural and controlled climatic conditions. |journal=Biocontrol Science and Technology |volume=20 |issue=1 |pages=25–36 |bibcode=2010BioST..20...25O |doi=10.1080/09583150903337805 |s2cid=85239942}}</ref> and red clover rust, [[Uromyces trifolii-repentis var. fallens|''Uromyces trifolii-repentis'' var. ''fallens'']]. Other problems include parasitic [[nematode]]s (roundworms) and viruses.{{citation needed|date=July 2022}}
''Trifolium pratense''<nowiki/>'s perennial nature affords sustained, reliable growth. Furthermore, the species' ability to [[nitrogen fixation|fix nitrogen]] promotes protein rich growth, supporting a wide range of wildlife including deer, turkeys, and rabbits.{{citation needed|date=May 2022}}
== Uses ==
It is widely grown as a [[fodder]] crop, valued for its [[nitrogen fixation]], which increases soil fertility. For these reasons, it is used as a [[green manure]] crop. Several [[cultivar group]]s have been selected for agricultural use, mostly derived from ''T. pratense'' var. ''sativum''. It has become naturalised in many temperate areas, including the Americas and [[Australasia]] as an escape from cultivation. The red clover has become increasingly important as a source of economic stability in Chile, which has made the need for pollinators even more important.<ref>{{Cite journal|title = The Introduction of Bombus Ruderatus to Chile for Red Clover Pollination|journal = Bee World|date = 1986-01-01|issn = 0005-772X|pages = 15–22|volume = 67|issue = 1|doi = 10.1080/0005772X.1986.11098855|first1 = P. V.|last1 = Arretz|first2 = R. P.|last2 = Macfarlane | bibcode=1986BeeW...67...15A }}</ref>
In India the highest producer of red clover seed is the Agriculture Department of Kashmir's Fodder Seed Production Station Aru.<ref name="Kashmir Mirror 2022">{{cite news | title=Director Agriculture Kashmir Choudhary Mohammad Iqbal visited Aru, Pahalgam | work=Kashmir Mirror | date=2022-02-20 |url=https://kashmirmirror.com/director-agriculture-kashmir-choudhary-mohammad-iqbal-visited-aru-pahalgam-2/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220220145630/https://kashmirmirror.com/director-agriculture-kashmir-choudhary-mohammad-iqbal-visited-aru-pahalgam-2/ |url-status=usurped |archive-date=February 20, 2022 | access-date=2022-07-01}}</ref> Two red clover accessions were deposited in the National Gene Bank of India in 2019 by the [[Indian Council of Agricultural Research]].<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://kashmirmirror.com/2021/10/17/director-agriculture-kashmir-inaugurates-41-varieties-of-high-yielding-fodder-crops-at-fodder-seed-production-farm-aru/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220820180829/https://kashmirmirror.com/2021/10/17/director-agriculture-kashmir-inaugurates-41-varieties-of-high-yielding-fodder-crops-at-fodder-seed-production-farm-aru/|url-status=usurped|archive-date=August 20, 2022|title=Director Agriculture Kashmir Inaugurates 41 varieties of high yielding Fodder Crops at Fodder Seed Production Farm Aru|work=Kashmir Mirror|date=October 17, 2021}}</ref>
It is also grown as an [[ornamental plant]]. Red clover's flowers and leaves are edible, and can be added as garnishes to any dish.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.ediblewildfood.com/red-clover.aspx|title=Red Clover: Pictures, Flowers, Leaves and Identification {{!}} Trifolium pratense|website=www.ediblewildfood.com|access-date=2019-02-15}}</ref> They can be ground into a [[flour]].
The flowers often are used to make [[jelly (fruit preserves)|jelly]] and [[tisane]]s, and are used in [[essiac]] recipes. Their [[essential oil]] may be extracted and its unique scent used in [[aromatherapy]].
The pink flowers afford high visibility levels and facilitate such attraction and may be used by wildlife remediation teams and conservationists seeking to build wildlife bridges to connect fragmented habitats.<ref>{{Cite web|date=2019-07-16|title=Wildlife Crossings|url=http://www.nationalgeographic.org/article/wildlife-crossings/|access-date=2021-01-22|website=National Geographic Society|language=en|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210203012404/http://www.nationalgeographic.org/article/wildlife-crossings/|archive-date=2021-02-03}}</ref>
===Cosmetics===
Extracts of red clover are used as cosmetic ingredients, and a number of preparations of the plant are listed under [[International Nomenclature of Cosmetic Ingredients|INCI]] names in the [[European Commission]]'s CosIng database of cosmetic ingredients. Trifolium Pratense Flower Extract (CosIng ref. 59842) is recorded with the functions astringent and fragrance,<ref name="CosIng59842">{{cite web |title=Ingredient: Trifolium Pratense Flower Extract |url=https://ec.europa.eu/growth/tools-databases/cosing/details/59842 |work=CosIng – Cosmetics Ingredients |publisher=European Commission |access-date=17 August 2026}}</ref> and Trifolium Pratense Leaf Extract (ref. 59840) as antioxidant and skin conditioning.<ref name="CosIng59840">{{cite web |title=Ingredient: Trifolium Pratense Leaf Extract |url=https://ec.europa.eu/growth/tools-databases/cosing/details/59840 |work=CosIng – Cosmetics Ingredients |publisher=European Commission |access-date=17 August 2026}}</ref> Neither entry records any provision under the Cosmetics Regulation or other restriction.<ref name="CosIng59842" /><ref name="CosIng59840" /> CosIng is a non-binding informational database, and inclusion in it does not constitute approval for use in cosmetic products; the regulatory status of a cosmetic ingredient in the [[European Union]] is determined by Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009 and its annexes.<ref name="CosIngNotice">{{cite web |title=Cosmetic ingredient database |url=https://single-market-economy.ec.europa.eu/sectors/cosmetics/cosmetic-ingredient-database_en |publisher=European Commission, Directorate-General for Internal Market, Industry, Entrepreneurship and SMEs |access-date=17 August 2026}}</ref>
===Folk medicine===
There is no good evidence red clover extracts are of any benefit for preventing or treating cancer or any other diseases.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.cancer.org/treatment/treatmentsandsideeffects/complementaryandalternativemedicine/herbsvitaminsandminerals/red-clover|title=Red Clover|date=November 2008|publisher=American Cancer Society|access-date=22 September 2013|archive-date=31 July 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140731172438/http://www.cancer.org/treatment/treatmentsandsideeffects/complementaryandalternativemedicine/herbsvitaminsandminerals/red-clover}}</ref><ref name="drugs">{{cite web |title=Red clover |url=https://www.drugs.com/npp/red-clover.html |publisher=Drugs.com |access-date=2 July 2026 |date=20 November 2025}}</ref> In [[alternative medicine]], red clover is promoted as a treatment for various disorders, having some evidence it may reduce the frequency of [[hot flash|hot flashes]] in [[Menopause|menopausal]] women.<ref name=drugs/><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Ullman |first1=Kristen E. |last2=Diem |first2=Susan |last3=Forte |first3=Mary L. |last4=Ensrud |first4=Kristine |last5=Sowerby |first5=Catherine |last6=Zerzan |first6=Nicholas |last7=Anthony |first7=Maylen |last8=Landsteiner |first8=Adrienne |last9=Greer |first9=Nancy |last10=Butler |first10=Mary |last11=Wilt |first11=Timothy J. |last12=Danan |first12=Elisheva R.| display-authors=3|date=2024 |title=Complementary and Alternative Therapies for Genitourinary Syndrome of Menopause: An Evidence Map |journal=Annals of Internal Medicine |language=en |volume=177 |issue=10 |pages=1389–1399 |doi=10.7326/ANNALS-24-00603 |issn=0003-4819 |pmc=12270004 |pmid=39250808}}</ref> Clinical organizations do not recommend use of red clover for treatment of menopause symptoms.<ref name=drugs/>

Systematic reviews specific to red clover have reported modest effects on hot flush frequency. A 2021 meta-analysis of eight randomised trials found a reduction of 1.73 hot flushes per day relative to placebo.<ref name="Kanadys2021">{{cite journal |last1=Kanadys |first1=Wiesław |last2=Barańska |first2=Agnieszka |last3=Błaszczuk |first3=Agata |display-authors=etal |title=Evaluation of clinical meaningfulness of red clover (Trifolium pratense L.) extract to relieve hot flushes and menopausal symptoms in peri- and post-menopausal women: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials |journal=Nutrients |volume=13 |issue=4 |pages=1258 |year=2021 |doi=10.3390/nu13041258 |doi-access=free |pmid=33920485 |pmc=8069620 }}</ref> A 2026 meta-analysis reported a small-to-moderate reduction in hot flush frequency.<ref name="Jiang2026">{{cite journal |last1=Jiang |first1=W. |last2=Wu |first2=K. |title=The effectiveness of red clover on hot-flash in menopausal women: a GRADE-assessed systematic review and meta-analysis |journal=European Journal of Obstetrics & Gynecology and Reproductive Biology |volume=324 |article-number=115226 |year=2026 |doi=10.1016/j.ejogrb.2026.115226 |pmid=42269521 }}</ref> A 2013 [[Cochrane (organisation)|Cochrane]] review of phytoestrogens found no difference between red clover extract and placebo in daily hot flush frequency.<ref name="Lethaby2013">{{cite journal |last1=Lethaby |first1=Anne |last2=Marjoribanks |first2=Jane |last3=Kronenberg |first3=Fredi |display-authors=etal |title=Phytoestrogens for menopausal vasomotor symptoms |journal=Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews |issue=12 |article-number=CD001395 |year=2013 |doi=10.1002/14651858.CD001395.pub4 |pmid=24323914 |pmc=10247921 }}</ref>

A 2015 assessment by the [[European Food Safety Authority]] of food supplements containing isolated [[isoflavone]]s, which included red clover isoflavones at the doses typically marketed to peri- and post-menopausal women, found no indication of adverse effects on the mammary gland, uterus or thyroid gland in post-menopausal women at the doses and durations studied.<ref name="EFSA2015">{{cite journal |author=EFSA Panel on Food Additives and Nutrient Sources added to Food (ANS) |title=Scientific Opinion on the risk assessment for peri- and post-menopausal women taking food supplements containing isolated isoflavones |journal=EFSA Journal |volume=13 |issue=10 |pages=4246 |year=2015 |doi=10.2903/j.efsa.2015.4246 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

In the United States, clover (''Trifolium'' spp.) is listed as [[generally recognized as safe]] for use as a spice or natural seasoning and flavoring; this listing does not extend to isoflavone supplement preparations.<ref name="CFR18210">{{cite web |title=21 CFR 182.10 – Spices and other natural seasonings and flavorings |url=https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/chapter-I/subchapter-B/part-182/subpart-A/section-182.10 |publisher=Electronic Code of Federal Regulations |access-date=17 August 2026}}</ref> The [[Food and Drug Administration]] has issued warning letters treating red clover products marketed with disease claims as unapproved new drugs.<ref name="FDA2017">{{cite web |title=Warning Letter: Everything Herbs |url=https://www.fda.gov/inspections-compliance-enforcement-and-criminal-investigations/warning-letters/everything-herbs-513211-04172017 |publisher=U.S. Food and Drug Administration |date=17 April 2017 |access-date=17 August 2026}}</ref>

===Phytochemistry===
[[Phytochemical]]s in red clover include [[carbohydrate]]s, [[isoflavone]]s and other [[flavonoid]]s, and [[saponin]]s.<ref name=drugs/> Isoflavones, also called [[phytoestrogen]]s, have structural similarity to [[estrogen]]s.<ref name=drugs/> The principal isoflavones are [[formononetin]], [[biochanin A]], [[daidzein]] and [[genistein]].<ref name="Booth2006">{{cite journal |last1=Booth |first1=Nancy L. |last2=Overk |first2=Cassia R. |last3=Yao |first3=Ping |display-authors=etal |title=The chemical and biologic profile of a red clover (Trifolium pratense L.) phase II clinical extract |journal=The Journal of Alternative and Complementary Medicine |volume=12 |issue=2 |pages=133–139 |year=2006 |doi=10.1089/acm.2006.12.133 |pmid=16566672 |pmc=1780253 }}</ref>

Isoflavone content varies markedly with plant part, phenological stage, cultivar and post-harvest processing.<ref name="Lemeziene2015">{{cite journal |last1=Lemežienė |first1=Nijolė |last2=Padarauskas |first2=Audrius |last3=Butkutė |first3=Bronislava |display-authors=etal |title=The concentration of isoflavones in red clover (''Trifolium pratense'' L.) at flowering stage |journal=Zemdirbyste-Agriculture |volume=102 |issue=4 |pages=443–448 |year=2015 |doi=10.13080/z-a.2015.102.057|doi-access=free }}</ref> [[Coumaric acid]] is a red clover component; due to its [[coumarin]] and flavonoid derivatives, ''T. pratense'' should be used with caution in individuals having [[coagulation]] disorders or prescribed with [[anticoagulation therapy]].<ref name=drugs/><ref>{{cite journal |author=W. Abebe |year=2002 |title=Herbal medication: potential for adverse interactions with analgesic drugs |journal=[[Journal of Clinical Pharmacy and Therapeutics]] |volume=27 |issue=6 |pages=391–401 |pmid=12472978 |doi=10.1046/j.1365-2710.2002.00444.x|s2cid=1828900 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

==In culture==
The red clover became the [[List of U.S. state flowers|state flower]] of [[Vermont]] in 1894.{{r|VHS|UVM Extension}} It has also been used as the [[Floral emblem|national flower]] of [[Denmark]]. In 1936 the Ministry of Foreign Affairs announced it was the national flower as part of an international exhibition taking place in Argentina. However, the choice did not become popular with the public. In 1987 the daisy, specifically either the [[marguerite daisy]] (''Argyranthemum frutescens'') or [[oxeye daisy]] (''Leucanthemum vulgare''), replaced it as the nation's floral emblem.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.ambwashington.um.dk/en/menu/InformationaboutDenmark/Culture/DanishNationalSymbols/Other+National+Symbols/ |title=Other National Symbols |publisher=Embassy of Denmark, Washington DC |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070517100210/http://www.ambwashington.um.dk/en/menu/InformationaboutDenmark/Culture/DanishNationalSymbols/Other+National+Symbols/ |archive-date=17 May 2007 |access-date=3 April 2015}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://naturstyrelsen.dk/om-os/kontakt/faq/nationalplanter-og-dyr/ |title=Nationalplanter og -dyr | publisher=Naturstyrelsen, Danish Ministry of the Environment |access-date=28 December 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230321144950/https://naturstyrelsen.dk/om-os/kontakt/faq/nationalplanter-og-dyr/ |archive-date=21 March 2023 |language=da |trans-title=Nationalplants and -animals }}</ref>
